intro: Think about the first thing a friend asks on Monday: What did you do this weekend? To answer in Spanish, you need the preterite, the past tense for actions that started and finished. Fui al cine (I went to the movies). Comimos pizza (We ate pizza). Mi hermana no quiso venir (My sister refused to come). Without it, you can only talk about what happens now.

This unit builds the preterite in two steps. First come the regular endings for -ar, -er and -ir verbs, the accent marks that separate hablo (I speak) from habló (he spoke), and the small spelling changes in llegué and empecé. Then come the irregular verbs you need most: fui, hice, tuve, dijo, pude. They break the pattern, but they break it in families, so you learn them in groups instead of one by one.

By the end, you will be able to tell a whole story about a day that already happened: a concert, a class trip, a family party. You will ask ¿Qué hiciste? and answer with the right endings, the right accents and the right time words. Many heritage speakers already say these forms at home; this unit shows you how to write them correctly.
bigQuestion: How do Spanish speakers signal that an action is finished, and how can you tell a complete story in the past?

words.d: the preterite — the past tense for actions that started and finished at a clear time
to speak — hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablasteis, hablaron
to eat — comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron
to live — viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivisteis, vivieron (same endings as -er)
the accent mark — habló (he spoke) versus hablo (I speak); regular yo and él forms carry it
yesterday — a time word that signals the preterite: Ayer trabajé (Yesterday I worked)
to arrive — yo llegué (g becomes gu before é); llegaste, llegó
to begin — yo empecé (z becomes c before é); empezó, empezaron
to go / to be — they share one preterite: fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron
to do, to make — hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicisteis, hicieron; no accents
to have — tuve, tuviste, tuvo, tuvimos, tuvisteis, tuvieron; tuve que means I had to
to say, to tell — dije, dijiste, dijo, dijimos, dijisteis, dijeron (no i after j)

test.q: Which sentence describes a finished action in the past?
choices: Canto en el coro los martes.
test.why: Canté is the yo preterite of cantar, and anoche (last night) marks a finished past moment.

test.q: Complete: Ayer mis primos ___ al parque. (caminar)
test.why: Ellos in the preterite of an -ar verb takes -aron: caminaron.

test.q: What does "Mi tía habló con la maestra" mean?
choices: My aunt speaks with the teacher.
I speak with my aunt's teacher.
My aunt spoke with the teacher.
My aunt will speak with the teacher.
test.why: Habló, with the accent on ó, is the él/ella preterite: she spoke.

test.q: Which nosotros form can only be past?
test.why: For -er verbs the present is bebemos and the preterite is bebimos, so bebimos is always past. The -ar and -ir forms look the same in both tenses.

test.q: Choose the correct form: Yo ___ a la escuela a las ocho. (llegar)
test.why: -gar verbs write gué in the yo preterite to keep the hard g sound: llegué.

test.q: Which yo form is spelled correctly?
test.why: -car verbs change c to qu before é: practiqué. The others should be busqué, empecé and almorcé.
The tú preterite ending for -er and -ir verbs is -iste, with no final -s: escribiste.
A tú question gets a yo answer. The yo preterite of comer is comí.

test.q: In "Fuimos a Pilsen y fue divertido," which verbs are used?
test.why: Fuimos a Pilsen has a destination, so it is ir. Fue divertido describes, so it is ser.

test.q: Which is the correct yo preterite of ir?
test.why: Fui is one syllable and takes no written accent.
Hacer uses the stem hic- plus -iste in the tú preterite: hiciste.

test.q: What does "No pude terminar la tarea" mean?
choices: I didn't want to finish the homework.
test.why: Pude is the yo preterite of poder; with no, it means I tried and could not.

test.q: Which form is correct for "they said"?
test.why: After the j-stem, the ellos ending is -eron: dijeron.

test.q: Complete: Mi hermano ___ diez horas anoche. (dormir)
test.why: Stem-changing -ir verbs change o to u only in the él and ellos preterite: durmió.

test.q: Which sentence has an accent error?
test.why: Irregular-stem preterites take no accent: tuvo. Regular forms like comió and llegué keep theirs.

write.prompt: Escribe un párrafo de 6 a 8 oraciones sobre un día especial del pasado: una fiesta, un viaje o un partido. Write about a real or invented day that already happened. Say where you went (fui), what you did (hice), what you ate, who came (vino) and how it was (fue). Use at least two time words like ayer, el sábado pasado or hace un mes.
tips: Use the verbs from this unit: fui, hice, tuve, comí, llegué, dijo.
Check every regular yo and él form for its accent: llegué, comió, habló.
Check that irregular forms have NO accent: hice, tuvo, fue, dijo.
Put a time word at the start of at least one sentence: Ayer, El sábado pasado.
Read it aloud and stress the last syllable of canté and cantó.

title: The Preterite: What Happened

chapters.title: Regular Preterite Endings
chapters.bigQuestion: How does one small ending, and sometimes one accent mark, tell a listener that something is already over?

story.title: Saturday Night at the Concert
story.kicker: Two friends retell a concert, and every verb they use points back to last Saturday.
paragraphs: On Monday morning, Daniela sat down next to her friend Marcos before first period. She could not stop smiling. "¿Qué hiciste el sábado?" (What did you do on Saturday?) Marcos asked. Daniela answered right away: "¡Fui a un concierto!" (I went to a concert!) Her cousin had bought tickets weeks before for a band from Chicago that sings in Spanish and English.

"Llegamos temprano" (We arrived early), she said. "Compré una camiseta y un refresco. Luego, la banda empezó a tocar." (I bought a T-shirt and a soda. Then the band started to play.) Every verb in her story pointed to finished moments: arriving, buying, starting. Marcos noticed that she never said compro (I buy); she said compré (I bought).

"¿Cantaste?" (Did you sing?) Marcos asked. "¡Sí! Canté todas las canciones. Mi prima bailó toda la noche." (Yes! I sang all the songs. My cousin danced all night.) Daniela explained that after the show they ate tacos near the venue. "Comimos tacos al pastor y volvimos a casa a la medianoche." (We ate tacos al pastor and went back home at midnight.)

Marcos laughed. "Yo no salí. Miré una película y dormí." (I didn't go out. I watched a movie and slept.) Two friends, two very different Saturdays, but the same tool carried both stories: the preterite, the Spanish past tense for actions that started and finished at a clear moment. In this chapter you will learn its regular endings, the accents that make them work, and the spelling changes hidden in the yo form.
story.think: Daniela used compré, canté and llegamos. What do these verbs have in common, and how would you tell a friend about your own last Saturday?

lessons.title: A Finished Action in the Past
lessons.mainIdea: The preterite tells about an action that happened and ended at a specific time in the past.
reading: Picture a friend asking what you did yesterday. You answer with actions that are done: you ate lunch, you studied, you called your grandmother. Spanish has a special tense for these finished actions, the *pretérito* (the preterite). A tense is a set of verb forms that shows time. The preterite answers the question "What happened?" with actions that have a clear start and end.

Compare two sentences. "Hablo con mi abuela" means I talk with my grandmother, now or usually. "Hablé con mi abuela anoche" means I talked with my grandmother last night, and the call is over. The stem habl- stays the same. Only the ending changes: -o for now, -é for a finished past. That single ending carries the whole idea of time.

The preterite is used for single events (Llegué a las ocho, I arrived at eight), for actions in a series (Entré, saludé y me senté, I came in, said hello and sat down), and for actions with a set length (Estudié dos horas, I studied for two hours). English speakers sometimes use "did" in questions, like "Did you study?" Spanish does not need an extra word: "¿Estudiaste?" already means Did you study?

words.d: the preterite — the Spanish past tense for completed actions with a clear beginning or end
to speak or talk — regular -ar verb; preterite yo form: hablé
to arrive — regular -ar verb; preterite: llegué, llegaste, llegó
to study — regular -ar verb; preterite: estudié, estudiaste, estudió

look.title: A Finished Evening
look.text: Yesterday: Llegué a casa a las cuatro. (I arrived home at four.) Estudié una hora. (I studied for an hour.) Hablé con mi abuela. (I talked with my grandmother.) Each action began, happened, and ended. None of them is still going on.
look.prompt: Name three things you did yesterday that had a clear end. Try saying one of them in Spanish with an -é ending.

check.q: Which sentence tells about a finished action in the past?
choices: Hablo con mi abuela los domingos.
Voy a hablar con mi abuela.
check.why: Hablé is the preterite yo form of hablar, and anoche (last night) sets a finished past moment.

check.q: What does "¿Estudiaste?" mean?
check.why: Estudiaste is the tú preterite form of estudiar, so it asks about a finished past action. Spanish needs no word for "did".

check.q: Which use fits the preterite best?
choices: An action that happens every day
An event that happened once and ended
check.why: The preterite is for completed actions with a clear start or end, like a single past event.

lessons.title: Time Words That Signal the Past
lessons.mainIdea: Words like ayer, anoche and la semana pasada are clues that a preterite verb is coming.
reading: When Marcos asked about Saturday, the word el sábado told Daniela to answer in the past. Spanish speakers use many time words like this. *ayer* means yesterday. *anoche* means last night. Anteayer means the day before yesterday. These words set the moment, and the preterite verb tells what happened at that moment.

Another group uses pasado or pasada, meaning last or past. The ending matches the noun: *la semana pasada* (last week) uses pasada because semana is feminine, while el año pasado (last year) and el mes pasado (last month) use pasado because año and mes are masculine. A common mistake is la semana pasado, which breaks gender agreement.

You can also count back with hace. "Hace dos días" means two days ago. "Visité a mi tía hace una semana" means I visited my aunt a week ago. Notice the word order: English puts ago at the end, but Spanish puts hace first, then the amount of time. Time words can start or end the sentence: "Ayer bailé" and "Bailé ayer" both mean I danced yesterday.

words.d: yesterday — often signals a preterite verb: Ayer trabajé (Yesterday I worked)
last night — Anoche miré una película (Last night I watched a movie)
last week — pasada agrees with the feminine noun semana
ago — hace tres días means three days ago; hace comes before the amount

look.title: Clues in a Text Message
look.text: Lucía texts her cousin: "Anoche cené con papá. Ayer compré zapatos. La semana pasada visité a la abuela. ¡Y hace un mes empecé mi trabajo nuevo!" (Last night I had dinner with Dad. Yesterday I bought shoes. Last week I visited Grandma. And a month ago I started my new job!)
look.prompt: Find each time word in Lucía's message. Which one would you use to talk about something you did seven days ago?

check.q: Choose the correct phrase for "last week."
check.why: Semana is feminine, so it takes la and the adjective pasada.

check.q: How do you say "two days ago" in Spanish?
check.why: Spanish puts hace before the amount of time: hace dos días.

check.q: What does "Anoche miré una película" mean?
choices: Last night I watched a movie.
Tonight I will watch a movie.
Every night I watch a movie.
Yesterday morning I watched a movie.
check.why: Anoche means last night, and miré is the preterite yo form of mirar (to watch).

lessons.title: Present or Preterite?
lessons.mainIdea: The ending of the verb, not the stem, tells you whether an action is happening now or already happened.
reading: Imagine you hear only one word from a conversation across the cafeteria: "Trabajó." Did someone work, or does someone work? The ending -ó with its accent tells you it is past: he or she worked. "Trabajo" without an accent would mean I work. Listening for endings is the key skill of this chapter.

Here is a side-by-side walk-through with *trabajar* (to work). Present: trabajo, trabajas, trabaja. Preterite: trabajé, trabajaste, trabajó. The stem trabaj- never changes. You drop -ar and add a new ending. Every preterite ending for yo and for él or ella in regular verbs carries a written accent, and that accent is stressed when you say it.

Time words help too. "Siempre trabajo los sábados" (I always work on Saturdays) is a habit, so it takes the present. "El sábado pasado trabajé seis horas" (Last Saturday I worked six hours) is one finished event, so it takes the preterite. When you write, look for a time word first, then choose the ending that matches it.

words.d: to work — present trabajo (I work), preterite trabajé (I worked)
the ending — the part of a verb added to the stem to show who and when
the stem — the part of the verb left after you drop -ar, -er or -ir, like trabaj-

look.title: Same Stem, Different Time
look.text:
Now: Trabajo en una tienda. (I work in a store.)
Past: Trabajé en una tienda el verano pasado. (I worked in a store last summer.)
Now: Ella trabaja mucho. (She works a lot.)
Past: Ella trabajó ayer. (She worked yesterday.)
look.prompt: Point to the ending that changes in each pair. Which pair uses an accent to mark the past?

check.q: Which verb form means "she worked"?
check.why: Trabajó, with -ó and an accent, is the él/ella preterite form of trabajar.

check.q: Which sentence needs the present tense, not the preterite?
check.why: Siempre (always) describes a habit, which takes the present tense.

check.q: In trabajé, what is the stem?
check.why: The stem is what remains after dropping -ar: trabaj-. The ending -é shows yo in the preterite.

lessons.title: The Six -ar Endings
lessons.mainIdea: Regular -ar verbs use -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis and -aron in the preterite.
reading: Daniela said "Canté todas las canciones" (I sang all the songs). Let's build the whole preterite of *cantar* (to sing). Drop -ar to get the stem cant-. Then add: yo canté, tú cantaste, él or ella or usted cantó, nosotros cantamos, vosotros cantasteis, ellos or ellas or ustedes cantaron.

Every regular -ar verb works the same way. Bailar (to dance): bailé, bailaste, bailó, bailamos, bailasteis, bailaron. *comprar* (to buy): compré, compraste, compró, compramos, comprasteis, compraron. If you know the six endings, you know hundreds of verbs, because most -ar verbs in Spanish are regular.

A frequent mistake is adding an extra -s to the tú form: "cantastes" instead of cantaste. You may hear cantastes in casual speech in some places, but standard written Spanish uses cantaste. Another mistake is mixing present and past: "Ellos cantan anoche" should be "Ellos cantaron anoche." The -aron ending marks ellos in the past.

words.d: to sing — canté, cantaste, cantó, cantamos, cantasteis, cantaron
to dance — Mi prima bailó toda la noche (My cousin danced all night)
to buy — Compré una camiseta (I bought a T-shirt)
to play an instrument; to touch — La banda tocó dos horas (The band played for two hours)

look.title: Building Cantar Step by Step
look.text:
cantar → drop -ar → cant-
yo cant + é = canté
tú cant + aste = cantaste
él/ella/usted cant + ó = cantó
nosotros cant + amos = cantamos
vosotros cant + asteis = cantasteis
ellos/ellas/ustedes cant + aron = cantaron
look.prompt: Use the same steps to build all six preterite forms of bailar. Which two forms need an accent?

check.q: Complete: Anoche ellos ___ en la fiesta. (bailar)
check.why: Ellos in the preterite takes -aron: bailaron.

check.q: Which is the standard tú preterite form of comprar?
check.why: The tú ending is -aste with no final -s: compraste.

check.q: What does "La banda tocó dos horas" mean?
choices: The band plays for two hours.
The band will play for two hours.
The band played for two hours.
The bands played for two hours.
check.why: Tocó is the él/ella preterite of tocar, and la banda is singular.

lessons.title: The Accent That Changes Meaning
lessons.mainIdea: Hablo means I speak, but habló means he or she spoke, so the written accent matters.
reading: Look at two words that seem almost the same: hablo and habló. In hablo, the stress falls on HA. In habló, the stress moves to the last syllable, LÓ, and the written *acento* (accent mark) shows that move. The first means I speak. The second means he, she or you (usted) spoke. One mark changes both the person and the time.

The same thing happens with the yo form. Hable, with no accent, is a command form (let him speak, or speak! to usted). Hablé, with the accent, means I spoke. So the accent on -é and -ó is not decoration. Leaving it off turns a past-tense sentence into a different sentence. Teachers mark this as a meaning error, not just a spelling error.

Practice by saying pairs aloud and stressing the final syllable in the preterite: compro and compró, estudio and estudió, llego and llegó. Heritage speakers often say these correctly without thinking but forget the accent when writing. A good habit is to check every yo and él form in the preterite before you turn in your work.

words.d: the accent mark — the written mark on é or ó that shows stress and can change meaning
the syllable — a beat in a word; ha-bló has two syllables and the stress is on the last one
he, she or you (usted) spoke — preterite of hablar; compare hablo (I speak)

look.title: Hear the Stress Move
look.text:
HA-blo → I speak (now)
ha-BLÓ → he or she spoke (past)
ES-tu-dio → I study
es-tu-DIÓ → she studied
LLE-go → I arrive
lle-GÓ → he arrived
look.prompt: Say each pair out loud and clap on the stressed syllable. Then write one sentence using llegó.

check.q: What does "Mi hermano habló con el maestro" mean?
choices: My brother speaks with the teacher.
I speak with my brother's teacher.
My brother will speak with the teacher.
My brother spoke with the teacher.
check.why: Habló, with the accent, is the él preterite form of hablar: he spoke.

check.q: Which word means "I studied"?
check.why: Estudié, with -é and an accent, is the yo preterite form. Estudio is I study, and estudió is he studied.

check.q: A student writes "Ayer ella llego tarde." What is wrong?
check.why: Without the accent, llego means I arrive. The past she arrived is llegó.

lessons.title: Nosotros: Same Form, Two Times
lessons.mainIdea: For -ar and -ir verbs, the nosotros form is the same in the present and the preterite, so context decides.
reading: Here is a surprise. "Hablamos" can mean we speak or we spoke. For -ar verbs, the nosotros form ends in -amos in both the present and the preterite. The form is identical, so Spanish speakers rely on context: the time words and the rest of the conversation.

"Hablamos todos los días" means we talk every day, a habit in the present. "Hablamos ayer" means we talked yesterday, a finished past action. The word ayer does all the work. The same is true for *caminar* (to walk): caminamos can mean we walk or we walked. Look for clues like ayer, anoche, el lunes pasado or hace una hora.

This is also true for -ir verbs: vivimos means we live or we lived. But -er verbs are different. In the present, we eat is comemos; in the preterite, we ate is comimos. So *comimos* can only be past. Daniela's line "Comimos tacos" had to be about Saturday night, even without a time word.

words.d: to walk — caminamos means we walk or we walked, depending on context
the context — the words and situation around a sentence that help show its meaning
we ate — preterite of comer; the present is comemos, so comimos can only be past

look.title: Which Time Is It?
look.text:
A: ¿Qué hacen ustedes los domingos? (What do you all do on Sundays?)
B: Caminamos en el parque. (We walk in the park.)
A: ¿Y el domingo pasado? (And last Sunday?)
B: Caminamos a la playa. (We walked to the beach.)
look.prompt: Caminamos appears twice with different meanings. What words in the dialogue tell you which time each one means?

check.q: In "Ayer caminamos al parque," what time does caminamos show?
check.why: Caminamos looks the same in present and preterite, but ayer (yesterday) makes it past.

check.q: Which nosotros form can ONLY be past?
check.why: For -er verbs the present is comemos and the preterite is comimos, so comimos is always past.

check.q: Choose the best translation: "Llegamos a las nueve anoche."
choices: We arrived at nine last night.
We arrive at nine every night.
We will arrive at nine tonight.
They arrived at nine last night.
check.why: Anoche (last night) makes llegamos past, and the -amos ending means we.

lessons.title: One Set of Endings for -er and -ir
lessons.mainIdea: Regular -er and -ir verbs share the preterite endings -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis and -ieron.
reading: After the concert, Daniela and her cousin ate tacos al pastor. Let's build *comer* (to eat) in the preterite. Drop -er to get com-. Add: yo comí, tú comiste, él or ella comió, nosotros comimos, vosotros comisteis, ellos comieron. Notice the i in every ending.

Now try *vivir* (to live). Drop -ir to get viv-. Add the very same endings: viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivisteis, vivieron. In the preterite, -er and -ir verbs are twins. That is good news: you learn one set of endings and use it for both groups.

Watch the accents again. Comí and comió both carry a written accent, just like canté and cantó. A common mistake is using -ar endings on an -er verb, like "comé" or "comó." Those are not Spanish words. Another is writing "comieron" as "comeron"; the ellos ending is -ieron, with the i before the e.

words.d: to eat — comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron
to live — viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivisteis, vivieron
to drink — Bebí un refresco (I drank a soda)
to write — Ella escribió una carta (She wrote a letter)

look.title: Twins in the Past
look.text:
comer → com-: comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron
vivir → viv-: viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivisteis, vivieron
The endings after the stem are identical. Only the stem is different.
look.prompt: Build the six preterite forms of escribir. Which forms carry a written accent?

check.q: Complete: Anoche yo ___ tacos al pastor. (comer)
check.why: The yo preterite ending for -er verbs is -í: comí.

check.q: Which form means "they lived"?
check.why: The ellos preterite ending for -ir verbs is -ieron: vivieron.

check.q: What does "Ella escribió una carta a su abuelo" mean?
choices: She writes a letter to her grandfather.
She wrote a letter to her grandfather.
I wrote a letter to her grandfather.
She will write a letter to her grandfather.
check.why: Escribió is the ella preterite form of escribir: she wrote.

lessons.title: Salir, Volver and Aprender in Action
lessons.mainIdea: The same -er and -ir endings let you tell a whole evening: going out, learning, and coming back.
reading: Marcos said "Yo no salí" (I didn't go out). *salir* (to go out, to leave) is irregular in the present yo form (salgo), but in the preterite it is completely regular: salí, saliste, salió, salimos, salisteis, salieron. Don't let a present-tense irregular scare you; check the preterite on its own.

*volver* (to return) is a stem-changing verb in the present: vuelvo, vuelves. In the preterite, -er stem changes disappear. You say volví, volviste, volvió, volvimos, volvisteis, volvieron, with the o from the infinitive. A common error is "vuelví," which mixes the present stem with a past ending.

Put them together and you can tell a night out: "Salimos a las siete. Aprendimos un baile nuevo. Volvimos a casa a las once." (We went out at seven. We learned a new dance. We came back home at eleven.) *aprender* (to learn) follows the pattern too: aprendí, aprendiste, aprendió. Three verbs, one set of endings, one clear story.

words.d: to go out, to leave — preterite is regular: salí, saliste, salió
to return, come back — preterite has no stem change: volví, volvió, volvieron
to learn — aprendí, aprendiste, aprendió, aprendimos, aprendieron

look.title: Marcos Tells His Evening
look.text: No salí el sábado. Comí pizza con mi hermana. Aprendí a jugar un videojuego nuevo. Mi mamá volvió del trabajo a las diez y todos bebimos chocolate caliente. (I didn't go out on Saturday. I ate pizza with my sister. I learned to play a new video game. My mom came back from work at ten and we all drank hot chocolate.)
look.prompt: List every preterite verb in Marcos's evening and give its infinitive.

check.q: Choose the correct form: Mi papá ___ a casa tarde. (volver)
check.why: -er verbs lose their stem change in the preterite, so the form is volvió.

check.q: Which is the yo preterite form of salir?
check.why: Salir is irregular only in the present yo (salgo). Its preterite is regular: salí.

check.q: What does "Aprendimos un baile nuevo" mean?
choices: We learn new dances every day.
We will learn a new dance.
check.why: Aprendimos is the nosotros preterite of aprender. For -er verbs, -imos is only past (present is aprendemos).

lessons.title: Asking and Answering About the Past
lessons.mainIdea: To answer a tú question in the preterite, switch the -aste or -iste ending to the yo ending -é or -í.
reading: Conversations about the past bounce between tú and yo. Marcos asked "¿Cantaste?" and Daniela answered "Canté." The question uses -aste, and the answer switches to -é. With -er and -ir verbs, "¿Comiste?" (Did you eat?) becomes "Sí, comí" (Yes, I ate). This switch is the most common move in real conversations.

A classic mistake is answering with the same form you heard: "¿Escribiste la tarea?" "Sí, escribiste." That answer means Yes, you wrote. You need escribí. When a teacher uses usted, the ending is -ó or -ió: "¿Terminó usted?" means Did you finish? and still takes a yo answer: "Sí, terminé."

To say no, put *no* before the verb: "No, no comí" (No, I didn't eat). The first no answers the question; the second makes the verb negative. English needs didn't, but Spanish just uses no plus the preterite. Question words work the same way: "¿Dónde comiste?" (Where did you eat?) "Comí en Pilsen" (I ate in Pilsen).

words.d: to finish — ¿Terminaste? (Did you finish?) Sí, terminé (Yes, I finished)
no, not — placed before the verb to make it negative: No comí (I didn't eat)
where? — ¿Dónde comiste? (Where did you eat?)
the homework — ¿Escribiste la tarea? (Did you write the homework?)

look.title: A Quick Exchange
look.text:
Mamá: ¿Terminaste la tarea? (Did you finish the homework?)
Hijo: Sí, terminé. (Yes, I finished.)
Mamá: ¿Comiste? (Did you eat?)
Hijo: No, no comí. (No, I didn't eat.)
Mamá: ¿Y llamaste a tu tía? (And did you call your aunt?)
Hijo: Sí, la llamé. (Yes, I called her.)
look.prompt: Write the son's answers if he did eat but did not call his aunt.

check.q: "¿Escribiste la tarea?" Choose the correct yes answer.
check.why: A tú question gets a yo answer. The yo preterite of escribir is escribí.

check.q: How do you say "I didn't eat"?
check.why: No goes before the verb, and comí is the yo preterite: No comí.

check.q: Your teacher asks "¿Terminó usted el examen?" What is she asking?
check.why: With usted, the -ó form means you (formal). She is asking whether you finished.

sections.title: Spelling Changes in the Yo Form

lessons.title: -car Verbs: Busqué and Toqué
lessons.mainIdea: Verbs ending in -car change c to qu in the yo preterite to keep the hard k sound: busqué, toqué.
reading: Say *buscar* (to look for) and listen to the hard k sound in bus-CAR. When you add the yo ending -é, the letters c + é would sound like s in most of the Spanish-speaking world, and the word would sound wrong. To keep the k sound, Spanish writes qu instead: busqué (I looked for).

This change happens only in the yo form. The other forms keep the c because the ending starts with a or o: buscaste, buscó, buscamos, buscasteis, buscaron. The same rule applies to *tocar* (to play an instrument): toqué, tocaste, tocó. And to *sacar* (to take out, to get a grade): saqué una A (I got an A).

This is not an irregular verb. The sound follows the regular pattern; only the spelling adjusts. Students often write "buscé" or "tocé." Say those aloud with Latin American pronunciation and you hear bus-SÉ, not bus-KÉ. The spelling change keeps the word's sound the same across all six forms.

words.d: to look for — yo form busqué; others keep c: buscaste, buscó
to play an instrument — yo toqué la guitarra (I played the guitar)
to take out; to get a grade — saqué una A (I got an A)
to practice — practiqué (I practiced), practicó (she practiced)

look.title: Keeping the K Sound
look.text:
buscar: bus-CAR (k sound)
busc + é → buscé? That would sound like bus-SÉ.
Fix: c becomes qu → busqué (bus-KÉ)
busc + ó → buscó (already sounds like k, no change)
Same move: tocar → toqué, sacar → saqué, practicar → practiqué
look.prompt: Why does buscó keep the c but busqué does not? Explain it in your own words.

check.q: Choose the correct form: Ayer yo ___ la guitarra. (tocar)
check.why: In the yo preterite, -car verbs change c to qu before é: toqué.

check.q: Which form does NOT change c to qu?
check.why: Only the yo form changes. Buscaste keeps c because the ending starts with a.

check.q: Why does sacar become saqué in the yo form?
choices: To keep the hard k sound before e
Because sacar is an irregular verb
To show that the subject is plural
Because all yo forms use qu
check.why: The spelling changes to keep the k sound; c before e would sound like s.

lessons.title: -gar and -zar Verbs: Llegué and Empecé
lessons.mainIdea: In the yo preterite, -gar verbs write gué and -zar verbs write cé: llegué, jugué, empecé, almorcé.
reading: Daniela said "Llegamos temprano," but if she were alone she would say "Llegué temprano" (I arrived early). *llegar* has a hard g sound. Before e, the letter g alone sounds like the Spanish j (a breathy h sound), so Spanish adds a silent u: llegué. The other forms stay plain: llegaste, llegó, llegaron. Jugar (to play a sport or game) works the same: jugué, jugaste, jugó. Pagar gives pagué.

Verbs ending in -zar change z to c before e. *empezar* (to begin) gives empecé (I began), but empezó (it began). *almorzar* (to eat lunch) gives almorcé. Here the sound does not change; Spanish spelling simply prefers ce over ze in most words, like cero and cena. Cruzar (to cross) gives crucé.

Put the three groups together with one memory line: car → qué, gar → gué, zar → cé, and only in yo. Other forms never change. A heritage speaker who says these words perfectly may still write "llegé" or "empezé" on a test. When you write the yo preterite of any verb ending in -car, -gar or -zar, stop and check the spelling.

words.d: to play a sport or game — jugué, jugaste, jugó; the u keeps the hard g
to begin, start — empecé (I began), empezó (it began)
to eat lunch — almorcé (I ate lunch), almorzaste, almorzó
to pay — pagué (I paid), pagó (he paid)

look.title: Example Receipt From the Concert
look.cite: Example prices made up for this lesson
look.prompt: Check the math: does 35 + 20 + 3 + 9 equal what Daniela paid? Then say in Spanish: I paid for the T-shirt (Pagué la camiseta).

check.q: Complete: Yo ___ al concierto a las siete. (llegar)
check.why: -gar verbs add u in the yo preterite to keep the hard g sound: llegué.

check.q: Which is the correct yo preterite of empezar?
check.why: -zar verbs change z to c before e, and there is no stem change in -ar preterites: empecé.

check.q: Which sentence is spelled correctly?
check.why: Jugó is the él form and needs no spelling change. The yo form would be jugué.

review.q: Which ending shows nosotros in the preterite of an -er verb?
review.why: -er and -ir verbs share -imos in the preterite: comimos, bebimos.

review.q: What does "Compraron boletos la semana pasada" mean?
review.why: -aron is the ellos/ellas/ustedes preterite ending, and la semana pasada means last week.

review.q: Choose the correct form: Anoche tú ___ muy bien. (cantar)
review.why: The standard tú preterite ending for -ar verbs is -aste: cantaste.

review.q: Which pair shows the spelling change correctly?
review.why: -gar verbs add u before é in the yo form: pagué.

review.q: Which sentence uses the preterite correctly?
choices: Ayer mi mamá trabajó ocho horas.
review.why: Ayer marks a finished past day, and trabajó is the ella preterite form.

review.q: Why is "Mi papá hablo con la maestra ayer" a mistake?
choices: Hablo means I speak; the past he spoke is habló.
Ayer cannot go at the end.
review.why: The accent moves the stress and changes the meaning: habló is he spoke.

review.q: Choose the correct form: Mi hermana ___ del trabajo a las seis. (volver)
review.why: -er stem changes do not happen in the preterite, and ella takes -ió: volvió.

review.q: Which yo preterite form is spelled correctly?
review.why: Sacar changes c to qu before é: saqué. The others should be practiqué, almorcé and empecé.

chapters.title: Irregular Preterites
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do the most common verbs break the preterite pattern, and how can a few small groups make them easy to remember?

story.title: Three Voices From the Field Museum
story.kicker: Three classmates tell the same museum trip, and the verbs they need most are the ones that break the rules.
paragraphs: On Friday, a Spanish class from a high school on the Southwest Side took the bus to the Field Museum in Chicago. On Monday, their teacher asked three students to tell the class what happened, en español. Jazmín went first. "Fuimos al museo el viernes. Fue un día increíble." (We went to the museum on Friday. It was an incredible day.)

Jazmín kept going. "Vimos el esqueleto de Sue, el tiranosaurio. Yo hice muchas fotos y mi amiga dijo que Sue es enorme." (We saw the skeleton of Sue, the T. rex. I took a lot of photos, and my friend said that Sue is huge.) The teacher smiled and wrote fuimos, fue, vimos, hice and dijo on the board. None of them followed the endings the class had just learned.

Kevin spoke next. "Yo no pude ver todo. Tuve que esperar en una fila muy larga y estuve allí media hora." (I couldn't see everything. I had to wait in a very long line, and I was there for half an hour.) Then Ana added her part: "Leí todos los carteles. Pedí un sándwich en la cafetería y en el autobús, Kevin durmió." (I read all the signs. I ordered a sandwich in the cafeteria, and on the bus, Kevin slept.) Everyone laughed, even Kevin.

The teacher pointed to the board. "These verbs are irregular in the preterite," she said, "but they are not random. They come in families." Some share forms, like ser and ir. Some use new stems, like tuv-, pud- and hic-. Some change a letter, like leyó, or a vowel, like durmió. In this chapter you will learn each family so you can tell your own story about a day out.
story.think: Which verbs in the students' stories did you already recognize? Which ones surprised you, and why might the most common verbs be the most irregular?

lessons.title: Fui, Fuiste, Fue: Two Verbs Share
lessons.mainIdea: Ser (to be) and ir (to go) have the same preterite forms: fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron.
reading: Jazmín said "Fuimos al museo" (We went to the museum) and then "Fue un día increíble" (It was an incredible day). The word fuimos comes from *ir* (to go). The word fue comes from *ser* (to be). In the preterite, these two very different verbs use exactly the same six forms.

Here is the full set: yo fui, tú fuiste, él or ella or usted fue, nosotros fuimos, vosotros fuisteis, ellos or ustedes fueron. Notice that fui and fue have no written accent. They are one-syllable words, so they need no accent. Writing "fuí" or "fué" is a common mistake; the accent was dropped from these words in the official spelling rules long ago.

The ending pattern is also odd. The ellos form is fueron, not "fuieron." Students sometimes try to make fue look regular by writing "fuió," which is not a word. The easiest approach is to memorize the six forms as a chant: fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron. You will use them in almost every story about the past.

words.d: to go — preterite: fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron
to be (identity, description, events) — same preterite as ir: fue un día increíble
the museum — Fuimos al museo (We went to the museum)
he, she or it went, or was — preterite of ir and ser; no written accent

look.title: One Set, Two Meanings
look.text:
Fui al museo. (I went to the museum.) — ir
Fui el primero en la fila. (I was the first in line.) — ser
Fuimos en autobús. (We went by bus.) — ir
Fue divertido. (It was fun.) — ser
The forms are identical. The rest of the sentence tells you which verb it is.
look.prompt: Write two sentences with fue, one meaning went and one meaning was.

check.q: Which is the correct yo preterite of ir?
check.why: The yo form is fui, with no written accent because it is one syllable.

check.q: Complete: Mis amigos ___ al partido el sábado. (ir)
check.why: The ellos preterite of ir is fueron.

check.q: What does "Fue un viaje largo" mean?
choices: He went on a long trip.
I went on a long trip.
check.why: Here fue comes from ser: It was a long trip. Un viaje largo describes what it was.

lessons.title: Telling Ser and Ir Apart
lessons.mainIdea: When you see fui or fue, look for a or a place to spot ir, and a description or noun to spot ser.
reading: Because ser and ir share forms, you read them by their neighbors. Ir almost always has a place or a direction. The little word *a* (to) is a strong clue: "Fue a la biblioteca" means she went to the library. Question words help too: "¿Adónde fuiste?" (Where did you go?) must be ir.

Ser usually comes with a description, a job, or an event. "Fue fácil" means it was easy. "Fue mi maestra" means she was my teacher. "¿Cómo fue el concierto?" means How was the concert? There is no destination, so it is ser. Think: is someone going somewhere, or is something being described?

Here is a tricky one: "Fui al concierto y fue genial." The first fui is ir (I went to the concert) because of al. The second fue is ser (it was great) because genial is a description. English speakers sometimes translate every fue as went. Slow down and check the words after the verb.

words.d: to — shows direction; fue a Pilsen means he went to Pilsen, so the verb is ir
to where? — ¿Adónde fuiste? (Where did you go?) always takes ir
great, awesome — El concierto fue genial (The concert was great)

look.title: Detective Work
look.text:
1. Fuimos a Humboldt Park el domingo.
2. La fiesta fue muy divertida.
3. ¿Adónde fueron tus padres?
4. Mi abuelo fue carpintero.
5. Fui al mercado y fue un desastre.
look.prompt: For each sentence, decide whether the verb is ser or ir, and name the clue that told you.

check.q: In "Mi abuela fue enfermera," which verb is fue?
choices: ser, because enfermera is a job
check.why: A job describes who someone was, so fue comes from ser: My grandmother was a nurse.

check.q: What does "¿Adónde fuiste ayer?" mean?
choices: Where do you go every day?
check.why: ¿Adónde? asks about a destination, so fuiste is from ir: Where did you go?

check.q: Translate: "Fui al cine y fue aburrido."
choices: I went to the movies and it was boring.
I was at the movies and he went, bored.
I go to the movies and it is boring.
He went to the movies and I was bored.
check.why: Fui + al is ir (I went); fue + aburrido is ser (it was boring).

lessons.title: Dar and Ver: Short and Accent-Free
lessons.mainIdea: Dar uses -er/-ir endings (di, dio) and ver is regular (vi, vio), and none of their one-syllable forms take an accent.
reading: Jazmín said "Vimos el esqueleto de Sue" (We saw Sue's skeleton). *ver* (to see) uses the regular -er endings: vi, viste, vio, vimos, visteis, vieron. The only surprise is that vi and vio have no accent. Like fui and fue, they are one syllable, so they need none.

*dar* (to give) is an -ar verb, but in the preterite it borrows the -er/-ir endings: di, diste, dio, dimos, disteis, dieron. A student guessing from the -ar pattern would write "dé" or "dó," which are wrong here. Think of dar as a verb dressed in ver's clothes: di and vi, dio and vio.

Dar is common in useful phrases. "Le di un regalo a mi mamá" means I gave my mom a gift. "El guía nos dio un mapa" means the guide gave us a map. Ver shows up whenever you describe a trip: "¿Qué viste?" (What did you see?) "Vi dinosaurios, momias y piedras preciosas" (I saw dinosaurs, mummies and gemstones).

words.d: to see — vi, viste, vio, vimos, visteis, vieron (no accents on vi, vio)
to give — uses -er/-ir endings: di, diste, dio, dimos, disteis, dieron
the guide (a male guide; la guía for a woman) — El guía nos dio un mapa
the skeleton — Vimos el esqueleto de un dinosaurio

look.title: At the Museum Entrance
look.text:
Guía: ¡Bienvenidos! Aquí tienen un mapa. (Welcome! Here is a map.)
Kevin, later: El guía nos dio un mapa, pero yo no vi nada al principio. (The guide gave us a map, but I didn't see anything at first.)
Ana: Yo vi a Sue primero. Le di mi mapa a Kevin. (I saw Sue first. I gave my map to Kevin.)
look.prompt: Find every form of dar and ver. Which ones would a student likely misspell with an accent?

check.q: Complete: El guía nos ___ un mapa. (dar)
check.why: Dar takes -er/-ir endings in the preterite, and dio is one syllable, so no accent.

check.q: What does "¿Qué viste en el museo?" mean?
choices: What do you see in the museum?
What did he see in the museum?
What did you wear to the museum?
What did you see in the museum?
check.why: Viste is the tú preterite of ver: What did you see? (Vestir, to dress, would be vestiste.)

check.q: Which is the ellos preterite of dar?
check.why: Dar borrows the -er/-ir ending -ieron: dieron.

lessons.title: Hacer: Hice and Hizo
lessons.mainIdea: Hacer uses the stem hic- and special endings: hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicisteis, hicieron.
reading: The question "¿Qué hiciste?" (What did you do?) opens almost every conversation about the past. It uses *hacer* (to do, to make), one of the most important irregular verbs. Its preterite stem is hic-, not hac-. The forms are hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicisteis, hicieron.

Look closely at two things. First, hice and hizo end in -e and -o with no accent. Irregular-stem preterites do not stress the last syllable, so they need no accent mark. Second, hizo is spelled with z, not c. If you wrote "hico," the c before o would sound like k. Spanish uses z to keep the s sound (in Latin America) before o.

Hacer answers and asks. "¿Qué hizo tu hermano?" (What did your brother do?) "Hizo la tarea y luego hizo la cena" (He did his homework and then made dinner). Note that the answer to a hacer question often uses another verb: "¿Qué hiciste el sábado?" "Fui a la playa." You don't need to repeat hacer in the answer.

words.d: to do, to make — hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicisteis, hicieron
he, she or you (usted) did or made — spelled with z; no accent
dinner — Mi papá hizo la cena (My dad made dinner)

look.title: Walk Through Hacer
look.text:
Stem: hac- changes to hic-
yo hic + e = hice (no accent)
tú hic + iste = hiciste
él/ella hic + o → hizo (c changes to z to keep the s sound)
nosotros hicimos · vosotros hicisteis · ellos hicieron
look.prompt: Ask a partner ¿Qué hiciste anoche? and answer with two different verbs.

check.q: Complete: ¿Qué ___ tú el fin de semana? (hacer)
check.why: The tú preterite of hacer uses the stem hic- plus -iste: hiciste.

check.q: Which is spelled correctly?
check.why: The él/ella form is hizo: z keeps the s sound, and irregular stems take no accent.

check.q: "¿Qué hicieron ustedes?" Which answer fits best?
check.why: A question to ustedes gets a nosotros answer in the preterite: hicimos.

lessons.title: The U-Stem Group
lessons.mainIdea: Tener, estar, poder and poner take u-stems (tuv-, estuv-, pud-, pus-) and the endings -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron.
reading: Kevin said "Tuve que esperar" (I had to wait) and "Estuve allí media hora" (I was there half an hour). These verbs belong to a family with a u in the preterite stem. *tener* becomes tuv-, *estar* becomes estuv-, *poder* becomes pud-, and poner becomes pus-.

All of them take the same special endings: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. So tener gives tuve, tuviste, tuvo, tuvimos, tuvisteis, tuvieron. Poder gives pude, pudiste, pudo, pudimos, pudisteis, pudieron. The yo and él forms end in plain -e and -o with no accent. Writing "tuvé" or "pudó" is the most common error here.

Some of these verbs shift meaning in the preterite. "No pude ver todo" means I couldn't see everything, in the sense that I tried and failed. "Tuve que esperar" means I had to wait, and I did. Estar in the preterite tells how long someone was somewhere: "Estuvimos en el museo cinco horas" (We were at the museum for five hours).

words.d: to have — tuve, tuviste, tuvo; tuve que means I had to (and did)
to be (location, condition) — estuve, estuviste, estuvo, estuvieron
to be able to — pude, pudo; no pude means I couldn't (I tried and failed)
to put — puse, pusiste, puso, pusieron

look.title: Example Timeline of the Trip
rows: minutos en la fila de Kevin
look.cite: Example schedule made up for this lesson
look.prompt: If the class arrived at 10:00 and estuvo en el museo cinco horas, at what time did they leave? Say it in Spanish with salieron.

check.q: Complete: Ayer yo ___ que trabajar. (tener)
check.why: Tener uses the stem tuv- and the yo ending -e, with no accent: tuve.

check.q: What does "No pudimos entrar" mean?
choices: We didn't want to go in.
check.why: Pudimos is the nosotros preterite of poder; with no, it means we tried and could not.

check.q: Which form is correct for "they were at the museum"?
check.why: Estar uses the stem estuv- and the ending -ieron: estuvieron. Location uses estar, not ser.

lessons.title: The I-Stem Group: Vine and Quise
lessons.mainIdea: Venir and querer take i-stems in the preterite: vine, vino, vinieron and quise, quiso, quisieron.
reading: Some irregular verbs change their stem vowel to i. *venir* (to come) becomes vin-: vine, viniste, vino, vinimos, vinisteis, vinieron. *querer* (to want) becomes quis-: quise, quisiste, quiso, quisimos, quisisteis, quisieron. They use the same accent-free endings as the u-stem group.

Be careful with vino. It is also the noun meaning wine, but in a sentence like "Mi prima vino al museo" it means my cousin came to the museum. Context makes it clear. Another trap is mixing up the present and past: vengo (I come) versus vine (I came). The g appears only in the present yo form.

Querer changes meaning in the preterite. "Quise llamarte" means I tried to call you. "No quiso comer" means he refused to eat, not just that he didn't feel like it. So Kevin could say "No quise esperar, pero tuve que esperar" (I didn't want to wait, but I had to wait). The preterite makes wanting sound like a decision.

words.d: to come — vine, viniste, vino, vinimos, vinisteis, vinieron
to want — quise (I tried), no quiso (he refused)
he, she or you came — preterite of venir; also the noun el vino (wine)

look.title: Who Came, Who Refused
look.text:
Maestra: ¿Quién vino tarde hoy? (Who came late today?)
Ana: Kevin vino tarde. (Kevin came late.)
Kevin: ¡Quise llegar temprano! Pero el autobús no vino. (I tried to arrive early! But the bus didn't come.)
Maestra: ¿Y tu hermano? (And your brother?)
Kevin: No quiso venir. (He refused to come.)
look.prompt: Explain the difference between No quiso venir and No quería venir as best you can: which sounds like a decision?

check.q: Complete: Mis tíos ___ a la fiesta. (venir)
check.why: Venir uses the stem vin- and the ellos ending -ieron: vinieron.

check.q: What does "Mi hermanito no quiso comer" mean?
choices: My little brother refused to eat.
My little brother doesn't want to eat.
I didn't want my little brother to eat.
check.why: No quiso in the preterite shows a refusal: he refused to eat.

check.q: Which form means "I came"?
check.why: The yo preterite of venir is vine, with no accent. Vengo is the present.

lessons.title: Decir and the J-Stem
lessons.mainIdea: Decir and traer take j-stems, and their ellos form drops the i: dijeron and trajeron.
reading: Jazmín reported that "mi amiga dijo que Sue es enorme" (my friend said that Sue is huge). *decir* (to say, to tell) uses the stem dij-: dije, dijiste, dijo, dijimos, dijisteis, dijeron. *traer* (to bring) uses traj-: traje, trajiste, trajo, trajimos, trajisteis, trajeron.

Look at the ellos form. After j, the ending is -eron, not -ieron. So it is dijeron, not "dijieron." This mistake is very common, even among fluent speakers, but standard Spanish writes dijeron and trajeron. The rule: when the stem ends in j, drop the i.

Decir is the verb of reporting. "Me dijo la verdad" means he told me the truth. "¿Qué dijiste?" means What did you say? Traer shows up on trips and at parties: "Traje mi almuerzo" (I brought my lunch). "¿Quién trajo la cámara?" (Who brought the camera?) Both verbs use no accent in yo and él forms.

words.d: to say, to tell — dije, dijiste, dijo, dijimos, dijisteis, dijeron
to bring — traje, trajiste, trajo, trajimos, trajisteis, trajeron
the truth — Me dijo la verdad (He told me the truth)
the lunch — Traje mi almuerzo (I brought my lunch)

look.title: Reporting What People Said
look.text:
The guide: "Sue es el tiranosaurio más famoso."
Jazmín reports it: El guía dijo que Sue es el tiranosaurio más famoso. (The guide said Sue is the most famous T. rex.)
Kevin: ¿Qué dijeron tus amigos? (What did your friends say?)
Ana: Dijeron que trajeron sus cámaras. (They said they brought their cameras.)
look.prompt: Report something a friend or teacher said to you today, starting with Dijo que or Me dijo que.

check.q: Choose the standard written form: Ellos ___ la verdad. (decir)
check.why: After a j-stem, the ellos ending is -eron: dijeron.

check.q: What does "¿Quién trajo la cámara?" mean?
check.why: Trajo is the él/ella preterite of traer (to bring).

check.q: Which yo form is correct?
check.why: Traer uses the stem traj- and the yo ending -e with no accent: traje.

lessons.title: I to Y: Leyó and Creyó
lessons.mainIdea: In leer, creer and oír, the i of -ió and -ieron becomes y between vowels: leyó, leyeron, creyó, oyó.
reading: Ana said "Leí todos los carteles" (I read all the signs). Try building *leer* (to read) with the regular endings. The stem is le-. Yo: leí. Tú: leíste. But for él, le- + ió would give three vowels in a row, "leió." Spanish changes that unstressed i to y: leyó. The ellos form becomes leyeron.

*creer* (to believe) and oír (to hear) follow the same rule: creyó, creyeron; oyó, oyeron. The other forms add written accents to keep the i as its own syllable: leí, leíste, leímos, leísteis; creí, creíste, creímos. Without the accent, leíste would be read as one blended sound.

These are not irregular verbs in meaning or stem. They follow the regular endings, and spelling simply keeps them pronounceable. A good tip: whenever the stem ends in a vowel and the ending is -ió or -ieron, expect a y. "Mi abuela leyó el periódico" (My grandmother read the newspaper). "¿Oyeron la música?" (Did you all hear the music?)

words.d: to read — leí, leíste, leyó, leímos, leísteis, leyeron
to believe — creí, creíste, creyó, creyeron
to hear — oí, oíste, oyó, oímos, oísteis, oyeron
the sign, poster — Leí todos los carteles (I read all the signs)

look.title: Too Many Vowels
look.text:
leer → stem le-
le + ió → leió? Three vowels in a row.
Fix: the i between vowels becomes y → leyó
le + ieron → leyeron
le + í → leí (accent keeps two syllables: le-í)
Same for creer: creyó, creyeron.
look.prompt: Use the rule to build the él and ellos forms of oír. Then check the accents on the other forms.

check.q: Complete: Ana ___ todos los carteles. (leer)
check.why: Between vowels, the i of -ió becomes y: leyó.

check.q: Which form means "they believed"?
check.why: Creer takes -eron with a y: creyeron.

check.q: Which yo form of leer is spelled correctly?
check.why: The accent on í keeps le-í as two syllables: leí.

lessons.title: Stem-Changing -ir Verbs: Durmió and Pidió
lessons.mainIdea: Stem-changing -ir verbs change in the él and ellos preterite only: o→u (durmió) and e→i (pidió).
reading: Ana joked that "en el autobús, Kevin durmió" (on the bus, Kevin slept). *dormir* (to sleep) has a stem change in the present (duermo). In the preterite, -ar and -er verbs lose their stem changes, but -ir verbs keep a smaller change in two forms. The o becomes u only in él and ellos: dormí, dormiste, durmió, dormimos, dormisteis, durmieron.

*pedir* (to ask for, to order) does the same with e→i: pedí, pediste, pidió, pedimos, pedisteis, pidieron. Servir (to serve) gives sirvió and sirvieron. Preferir (to prefer) gives prefirió. Morir (to die) gives murió. Think of it as a change that appears only in the third person, both singular and plural.

Two mistakes are common. One is using the present stem in every form: "duermí" or "piediste." The other is forgetting the change in the third person: "Kevin dormió." Remember: yo, tú, nosotros and vosotros keep the infinitive stem, and only él and ellos change. "Pedí un sándwich y mi amiga pidió una sopa" (I ordered a sandwich and my friend ordered a soup).

words.d: to sleep — dormí, dormiste, durmió, dormimos, durmieron (o→u only in él and ellos)
to ask for, to order — pedí, pediste, pidió, pedimos, pidieron
to serve — sirvió, sirvieron in the third person
to prefer — preferí, prefirió, prefirieron

look.title: At the Museum Cafeteria
look.text:
Yo pedí un sándwich. (I ordered a sandwich.)
Jazmín pidió una ensalada. (Jazmín ordered a salad.)
Los chicos pidieron pizza. (The boys ordered pizza.)
Nosotros pedimos agua. (We ordered water.)
Después, Kevin durmió en el autobús. (Afterward, Kevin slept on the bus.)
look.prompt: Circle the forms that show a stem change. Which persons are they?

check.q: Complete: Kevin ___ en el autobús. (dormir)
check.why: Stem-changing -ir verbs change o to u in the él preterite: durmió.

check.q: Which form is correct for "I ordered"?
check.why: The yo form keeps the infinitive stem: pedí. Only él and ellos change to pid-.

check.q: Complete: Los meseros ___ la comida. (servir)
check.why: In the ellos preterite, servir changes e to i: sirvieron.

lessons.title: Telling the Whole Trip
lessons.mainIdea: A good story mixes regular and irregular preterites, so check each verb's family as you write.
reading: Now you can tell the whole museum trip. Start with the setting: "El viernes fuimos al Field Museum." Add actions in order with words like *primero* (first), luego (then) and *después* (afterward): "Primero vimos a Sue. Luego estuvimos en la sala de Egipto. Después comimos en la cafetería."

As you write, sort each verb into its family. Regular -ar: visitamos, caminamos. Regular -er/-ir: comimos, salimos. Ser/ir: fuimos, fue. New stems: hicimos, tuvimos, pudimos, vinieron, dijo. Spelling changes: llegué, leyó. Third-person stem change: durmió, pidió. Knowing the family tells you the ending and whether it needs an accent.

End with a reaction, which often uses ser: "Fue un día fantástico" (It was a fantastic day). Before you share, reread for the three biggest errors: missing accents on regular yo and él forms (llegó, comí), extra accents on irregular ones (hizo, tuvo, fue), and -ieron after j (dijeron, not dijieron). Those checks fix most mistakes.

words.d: first — Primero vimos a Sue (First we saw Sue)
then, next — Luego fuimos a la cafetería (Then we went to the cafeteria)
afterward, later — Después volvimos a la escuela (Afterward we returned to school)
the room, hall (in a museum) — la sala de Egipto (the Egypt hall)

look.title: Jazmín's Final Draft
look.text: El viernes fuimos al Field Museum en autobús. Primero vimos a Sue. Yo hice muchas fotos. Luego Kevin tuvo que esperar en una fila larga. Después Ana pidió un sándwich y todos comimos juntos. En el autobús, Kevin durmió. ¡Fue un día increíble!
look.prompt: Sort every verb in Jazmín's draft into its family: regular, ser/ir, new stem, or third-person change.

check.q: Which sentence has an accent error?
check.why: Irregular-stem forms take no accent. The correct form is hizo.

check.q: In "Luego estuvimos en la sala de Egipto," what does luego tell the reader?
check.why: Luego (then) is a sequence word that puts actions in order.

check.q: Which verb is in the correct family and form?
check.why: Pedir changes e to i in the ellos preterite: pidieron. The others should be dijeron, tuvimos and fui.

review.q: Which two verbs share the same preterite forms?
review.why: Ser and ir both use fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron.
Ver takes regular -er endings in the preterite: vimos.

review.q: Which form is correct for "she had"?
review.why: Tener uses the stem tuv- and the él/ella ending -o with no accent: tuvo.

review.q: What does "Mi hermano no pudo venir" mean?
choices: My brother doesn't want to come.
My brother didn't come in time.
review.why: No pudo is the preterite of poder: he wasn't able to come.
Between vowels, the i of -ieron becomes y: leyeron.
After a j-stem, the ellos ending is -eron: trajeron.

review.q: In "Fui a la tienda y fue fácil," which verbs are used?
review.why: Fui a la tienda has a destination (ir). Fue fácil is a description (ser).
Pedir changes e to i in the él/ella preterite: pidió.
